If they run it back at lightweight, Holloway is the more reliable side now. Conor’s best path is still the same: southpaw counter left hand, early reads, and trying to punish Max before the pace compounds. The problem is that Holloway has grown into exactly the kind of opponent who can survive the early danger, force high-volume exchanges, and steadily take over when the fight becomes a cardio-and-output test. Recent form matters a lot here. Conor’s last real stretch showed a big decline in durability and sustainability, especially after the Poirier losses and the long layoffs. Holloway is not coming in perfect either, but his recent run has been against elite opposition and his engine still looks like the key weapon. Even when he loses, he keeps operating at a pace that makes pure shot-selection fighters uncomfortable. Stylistically, this is a rougher matchup for McGregor in a second meeting than it was in the first. Conor was at his sharpest when opponents backed up in straight lines, but Holloway has improved at layering volume, changing looks, and entering combinations in waves. At 5'11 with a 69" reach, he gives up length, but he also tends to win the volume battle and drag the fight into extended exchanges where Conor has less room to land something clean and final. Holloway’s durability isn’t perfect, but he’s far more proven at living through adversity and reasserting himself. Finish profile favors Holloway by decision more than a late stoppage. Conor can still hurt anyone early, so the first round is the danger zone. But over 25 minutes, the more likely story is Holloway absorbing the best counters, pushing a higher pace, and banking rounds with pressure, combinations, and body work. If there’s a finish, it’s more likely Holloway by late TKO than Conor landing a clean early shot — but the safest prediction is Holloway on points. Key uncertainty: Conor’s one-punch threat is always real, and a fast start could flip the whole fight. If Holloway gets careless in the first 7-8 minutes, McGregor can absolutely make him pay. But over a full five rounds, I lean Holloway’s durability, volume, and cardio to win the rematch.

The O’Malley, Yan, and Cejudo fights told the same story: Song can hang with top-tier technical strikers, but he’s at his best when he increases volume, pushes the pace, and turns exchanges into attrition. Figueiredo is dangerous for as long as the fight stays fresh, but the style move up has made him more of a compact power threat than a true bankable 5-round bully at bantamweight. He still has 9 KOs and 9 subs, so the threat is real everywhere early, yet his last five show a tougher time against long, mobile, high-level 135ers. Against Umar he got shut down over three rounds, against Yan he was outpointed, and the Sandhagen fight ended with a knee injury after he was being forced to work hard. Style matchup favors Song’s youth, length, and pace. He’s got a slight reach edge on paper, better consistency in the pocket, and more upside in a prolonged striking battle. Figueiredo’s best path is an early burst, clinch damage, or catching Song in a scramble, but Song’s team at Alpha Male usually prepares him well for layered pressure and smart shot selection. Finish profile: Song is more likely to win by accumulation than a single-shot flash. Figueiredo is durable enough to extend this, but the weight of Song’s combinations, body work, and pace should start to break him in the championship rounds. Official pick: Paddy Pimblett
Method/time: Submission, Round 4, around 2:30
Confidence: 6.5/10

Why: Paddy’s recent form has aged well. He just went 5 hard rounds with Justin Gaethje, then before that showed real finishing progression with a third-round TKO of Michael Chandler and a quick technical submission of King Green. That tells you two things: his cardio is good enough to keep a dangerous pace, and his opportunistic grappling is still a major weapon when opponents overextend. Against BSD, that matters because St-Denis is aggressive, explosive, and very dangerous early, but he can also be drawn into scrambles and over-commit to pressure.

Style matchup: BSD is the stronger “must-fight-now” athlete here, with the nastier early finishing profile and a clear ability to hurt people fast. His run through Hooker, Dariush, Ruffy, and Prepolec shows he’s become much more than just a pressure grappler. But Paddy’s combination of composure, craft, and submission threat is the cleaner long-game answer. If he survives the first big storm, he should be able to make BSD work in longer exchanges, where Paddy’s pace management and opportunistic clinch/grappling transitions become more valuable.

Finish profile: BSD’s best window is rounds 1-2, especially if he can force chaos and make Paddy reset often. Paddy’s best window is rounds 2-4, when BSD’s pressure can become a little more open and Paddy can capitalize on scrambles, front headlock threats, and back takes.

Key uncertainty: BSD’s explosiveness is a real problem, and if he lands clean early he can absolutely flip the fight. The main swing factor is whether Paddy can stay disciplined through the first round without giving BSD the kind of layered grappling chaos that leads to top control or damage. If he does, I favor Paddy’s durability and submission game to take over late.
